title: Mobility, Velocity Saturation and Output Resistance
intro: High vertical and lateral fields lower carrier mobility, cap carrier velocity and heat carriers; and the output resistance is far from the constant that $\lambda$ suggests (Razavi, Sections 17.2.2 to 17.2.5).

blocks.text: A large gate voltage presses the carriers against the oxide interface, where they scatter more. An empirical model:

$\mu_0$ is the low-field mobility and $\theta$ a fitting parameter that grows as the oxide thins (Razavi quotes roughly 1 V$^{-1}$ for a 100 Å oxide), so mobility falls noticeably once the overdrive exceeds about 100 mV. Besides lowering current and $g_m$, it adds odd-order distortion to a square-law device. For $\theta V_{ov} \ll 1$:
Carrier velocity $v = \mu E$ stops growing at high lateral field, saturating near $10^7$ cm/s once fields approach 1 V/µm. If the whole channel were velocity-saturated:

linear in overdrive, independent of $L$, and with $g_m$ barely dependent on current or length. Real devices sit in between: the current saturates at $V_{D0} < V_{GS} - V_{TH}$, before pinch-off, at a lower level and with a lower $g_m$ than the square law predicts. A compact model valid in saturation:

blocks.alt: Normalised drain current against overdrive. The square-law curve is a parabola; the velocity-saturation curve follows it at small overdrive but bends toward a straight line at large overdrive, approaching a dashed linear asymptote.
blocks.caption: Square law against the velocity-saturation model.

blocks.text: Large $L$ or $v_{sat}$ gives back the square law; so does a small overdrive, since the denominator is then dominated by $2v_{sat}L/\mu$. For $L = 0.25$ µm and $\mu_0 = 350$ cm²/V·s that term is about 1.4 V, so overdrives of a few hundred millivolts stay nearly square-law. Folding in $\mu_{eff}$:
so lateral and vertical field effects add as one effective $\theta$, with the same distortion consequences.

Even when average velocity saturates, carriers near the drain keep gaining energy. These hot carriers can ionize silicon atoms on impact, creating electron-hole pairs: the electrons join the drain current and the holes flow to the substrate, a drain-to-substrate current. The most energetic can even tunnel into the gate oxide. Hot-carrier damage was a main reason supplies had to scale; at supplies near 1 V, a carrier cannot reach the 1.12 eV bandgap energy needed to create a pair, so the effect has largely faded in nanometer processes.

A single $\lambda$ assumes constant $r_O$. In reality, just past pinch-off the pinch-off region widens quickly with $V_{DS}$ (like a junction at low reverse bias), then more slowly, so $r_O$ rises with $V_{DS}$. At higher $V_{DS}$, DIBL lowers the threshold and roughly cancels the rise, giving a plateau. At still higher $V_{DS}$ impact ionization adds a drain-to-substrate current and $r_O$ falls.

blocks.alt: Output resistance against drain voltage: rising from the saturation edge, flattening into a broad maximum, then falling steeply at high drain voltage.
blocks.caption: Three regions of $r_O$: channel-length modulation, a DIBL-flattened plateau, and impact ionization.

blocks.text: Consequences: an op amp's gain changes with its output voltage (distortion), and in a cascode impact ionization sends current from drain to substrate rather than to the source, capping the achievable output resistance.

blocks.title: Mobility degradation
blocks.text: With $\theta = 1.5\text{ V}^{-1}$, how much lower is $\mu_{eff}$ than $\mu_0$ at 0.1 V and at 0.3 V overdrive?

blocks.title: How square is the law?
blocks.text: For a device with $L = 0.1\ \mu\text{m}$, $\mu_{eff} = 300\text{ cm}^2/\text{V·s}$ and $v_{sat} = 10^7\text{ cm/s}$, find $2v_{sat}L/\mu$ and the ratio of the velocity-saturated current to the square-law current at overdrives of 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5 V.
solution: Dividing the compact model by the square law gives $a/(V_{ov} + a)$ with $a = 0.67$ V: 0.87, 0.77 and 0.57.

blocks.title: Velocity-saturated transconductance
blocks.text: In full velocity saturation, what $g_m$ does a 10 µm wide device have with $C_{ox} = 15\text{ fF}/\mu\text{m}^2$ and $v_{sat} = 10^5$ m/s? What happens if you double its current by doubling the overdrive?
solution: Nothing: in this limit $g_m$ does not depend on current, so extra current buys no $g_m$.

blocks.title: Gain against output voltage
blocks.text: A single-stage amplifier has gain $g_mr_O$ with $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$. Its $r_O$ is 20 kΩ near the edge of saturation, 50 kΩ in mid-range and 15 kΩ near the top of the swing. What gain variation does that cause?
solution: Gain 40, 100 and 30: a 3:1 change across the swing, which shows up as distortion of large signals.
